title: Referred for vestibular rehab, with signs that point elsewhere
objective: Coordination and gait examination: the Romberg test with eyes closed for proprioception versus station with eyes open, and cerebellar ataxia as a cause of abnormal findings
secondaryObjectives: Differential diagnosis: distinguishing conditions appropriate for physical therapy from those requiring referral
Determining when a patient needs further examination, consultation or referral to another professional

Vestibular rehabilitation: supervised therapy for unilateral and bilateral hypofunction, gaze-stabilization doses from the guideline, and stopping when goals are met, symptoms resolve or progress plateaus
Determining a physical therapy diagnosis that guides management

brief.situation: 09:00 in an outpatient clinic. Mr. Whitfield, 67, arrives in a wheelchair pushed by his wife. Urgent care told him yesterday afternoon he had 'an inner ear infection' (vestibular neuritis) and referred him for vestibular rehabilitation. He is dizzy all the time.
handover: Referral: 'Vestibular neuritis, evaluate and treat.' No imaging was done. Meclizine prescribed.
History on the intake form: high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, smoker.
Clinic policy: a suspected stroke goes by 911 to the nearest stroke center; tell the referring provider the same day.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each test takes a minute or two. Decide what to test, what the findings mean and what to do.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: An evolving posterior circulation stroke: untreated, he worsens to vomiting and drowsiness near 09:30 and to a reduced level of consciousness near 09:40. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
He vomits and is harder to keep upright. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Drowsy and hard to rouse: an emergency in the clinic. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
A bedside oculomotor or coordination test: about 1 min.
EMS reaches the clinic about 10 min after a 911 call.

why.question: Is this vestibular neuritis? Which findings support or argue against it, and what do you do now?

parts.label: Central versus peripheral
parts.criteria: Argues against vestibular neuritis: new diplopia and slurred speech, direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, a normal head impulse in a patient with constant vertigo and nystagmus, severe gait and truncal ataxia (cannot stand feet together with eyes open, so not a Romberg sign of proprioceptive loss), limb ataxia; vascular risk factors and occipital headache; names a suspected posterior circulation stroke.
parts.modelAnswer: This does not look like vestibular neuritis. He has new double vision and slurred speech, nystagmus that changes direction with gaze, a normal head impulse despite constant vertigo and nystagmus, and he cannot stand feet together even with his eyes open or walk without holding on, plus left finger-to-nose ataxia. With high blood pressure, diabetes, smoking and an occipital headache, I suspect a posterior circulation stroke.

parts.label: Action
parts.criteria: Stops the vestibular exam and does not start gaze stabilization or positional tests; gait belt and close guarding for any standing; calls 911 now with the time last known well for transport to a stroke center (not a same-day office visit or a private car); stays with him; tells the referrer.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop the vestibular exam and do not start exercises or a Dix-Hallpike. Guard him with a gait belt if he has to stand. Call 911 now: suspected posterior circulation stroke, last known well yesterday at 07:00, to the stroke center. Stay with him, nothing by mouth, and tell the urgent care that referred him.

expertPath.text: Ask about double vision, speech and swallowing: new diplopia and slurred speech since yesterday. A red flag already.
Nystagmus in each direction of gaze: direction-changing. Head impulse: normal, which with constant vertigo argues against neuritis. Finger-to-nose: left ataxia.
Impression: central. Call 911 with the time last known well; stay with him; no exercises, no Dix-Hallpike, no walking test.
Tell the referring urgent care. EMS arrives about 09:14.

fall.headline: He fell
fall.body: Severe imbalance means a gait belt and close guarding before any standing or walking test, and with central signs the walking test may not be needed at all.

worsened.headline: He worsened in the clinic
worsened.body: Find when the first central sign appeared and how long it took to call 911.

sentFast.headline: Central signs found; sent by 911
sentFast.body: You screened for central signs, recognized that this was not vestibular neuritis, kept vestibular treatment out of it and called 911 with the time last known well. That is the expert path.

sentSlow.headline: Sent, by a slower or riskier route
sentSlow.body: Check the route (911, not a same-day office visit or a private car), how long after the first central sign you called, and whether exercises or positional tests were done.

time_up.headline: Still in the clinic
time_up.body: A referral diagnosis is a starting point. When the exam disagrees, act on the exam.

scoring.modelReasoning: A referral for vestibular neuritis does not settle the diagnosis. Acute constant vertigo with new diplopia and slurred speech, direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, a normal head impulse in the presence of constant vertigo and nystagmus, inability to stand feet together even with the eyes open (cerebellar, not the proprioceptive loss a Romberg test looks for) or to walk unaided, and limb ataxia point to a central cause, here a suspected posterior circulation stroke in a man with vascular risk factors. The vestibular hypofunction guideline does not apply; gaze stabilization and positional tests are not the plan. Guard any standing with a gait belt, call 911 with the time last known well for a stroke center, stay with him and tell the referring provider.

hitQ.ask: While you test: in someone with constant vertigo and nystagmus, what does a normal head impulse suggest?

choices.label: A central cause is more likely

hitQ.explain: In acute vestibular syndrome, an abnormal head impulse fits a peripheral loss; a normal one, with direction-changing nystagmus or a skew, points central. GRACE-3 asks for HINTS by trained clinicians and MRI for central or equivocal findings.
